MEDI2004 · Week 6 · Lecture 12

Drug Safety — Adverse Effects, Interactions & Poisoning

From the narrow gap between a therapeutic dose and a toxic one, through the hidden hazards of polypharmacy and CYP450 interactions, to the systematic approach for saving a poisoned patient — this guide decodes what makes drugs dangerous and what we do about it.

Covers Slides 1–28 (all content) Figures 8 plates from lecture Sections §0–§5

§0Epidemiology

The Scale of the Problem

Drug harm is the second most common adverse event in hospitals — and more than half of it is preventable.

Before learning how drugs cause harm, it is worth appreciating how large the problem is. Australia's Health data and the Standard 4 medication safety framework give us the numbers that motivate everything that follows in this lecture. Plate 0.1 shows adverse drug effects standing out as the second-largest category of hospital adverse events.

Label Key — Reading the AIHW bar chart
Adverse effects of drugs, medicaments and biological substances
~2 per 100 hospitalisations — second longest bar, highlighted with the red arrow. This is the category that encompasses adverse drug reactions, medication errors, and biological agent harms. It matters because it is the category most directly amenable to clinical intervention.
All adverse events
~5.3 per 100 — the reference bar. Drug harm sits second, meaning that for every 100 hospital admissions, approximately 2 are complicated by a drug-related adverse event.

The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (the body that sets Medication Safety — Standard 4) estimates that approximately 2–3% of all hospital admissions are medicine-related, and roughly 1.4% are specifically attributable to adverse drug reactions (ADRs) on admission. These figures are almost certainly under-reported. Critically, more than half of ADR-related admissions are considered preventable — meaning a working knowledge of what causes ADRs, and how to avoid them, has direct patient impact.

Reasoning · Why is drug harm so prevalent?

Drugs are biologically active molecules with intended targets — but biological systems are interconnected. A drug designed to slow the heart (beta-blocker) will also affect bronchial smooth muscle. One that reduces clotting (warfarin) sits perilously close to a dose that causes haemorrhage. The more drugs a patient takes, the more opportunities for these off-target effects to compound. Complicating matters, drug handling varies dramatically between patients: age, genetics, liver and kidney function, and co-medications all shift the dose-response curve relative to the "average" patient the drug was tested in.

Clinical context · The US benchmark

Makary & Daniel (BMJ 2016) estimated that medical error — a category dominated by medication errors — is the third leading cause of death in the United States. This figure shaped a global shift toward medication reconciliation, pharmacist review, and high-alert drug protocols in hospitals. It underscores why pharmacology is not just an exam topic but a patient-safety discipline.

R Recall — §0 The Scale of the Problem
  • 32% — drug/medication adverse events as a share of all adverse events in Australian hospitals (AIHW 2015-16)
  • 2–3% of hospital admissions are medicine-related; ~1.4% are ADRs on admission
  • More than half of ADR admissions are preventable
  • Medical error = 3rd leading cause of death in the US (Makary & Daniel, BMJ 2016)
§1Drug Safety Metrics

Therapeutic Index & Safety Window

How close is the dose that heals to the dose that harms? The therapeutic index answers this precisely.

To evaluate drug safety systematically, pharmacologists use two related but distinct concepts: the therapeutic index (a population-level ratio) and the therapeutic window (a clinical plasma-concentration target range). Understanding both is essential to recognising why some drugs demand careful monitoring.

§1.1Calculating the Therapeutic Index

Label Key — Therapeutic index dose-response curves
Blue S-curve (Therapeutic effect)
The dose–response relationship for benefit: as dose rises, the proportion of the population experiencing the therapeutic effect rises sigmoidally. At the ED50 dose, exactly 50% of patients are helped. The curve's shape reflects population variability in drug sensitivity.
Red S-curve (Toxic effect)
The dose–response relationship for harm: the same sigmoidal shape, but the curve is displaced rightward for a safe drug. At TD50, 50% of the population experience a toxic response. The steeper and closer to the blue curve, the more dangerous the drug.
ED50 (blue dashed vertical)
The effective dose in 50% of the population — read off where the blue curve crosses the 50% horizontal line. This is the denominator of the TI formula.
TD50 (red dashed vertical)
The toxic dose in 50% of the population — where the red curve crosses 50%. This is the numerator. A large gap between ED50 and TD50 means wide TI, i.e. a generous margin of safety.
Therapeutic index arrow
The horizontal distance between the two vertical lines at the 50% level. As Plate 1.1 shows, the TI is the ratio of these two doses — a dimensionless number that quantifies safety margin.

As Plate 1.1 shows, the Therapeutic Index (TI) is defined as:

Worked example · Calculating the Therapeutic Index

Given: ED50 = 10 mg and TD50 = 60 mg. Calculate the TI and interpret its clinical meaning.

  1. State the formula: TI = TD50 / ED50. The TI is a ratio — the higher it is, the greater the separation between effective and toxic doses.
  2. Substitute values: TI = 60 mg / 10 mg = 6
  3. Interpret: A TI of 6 means the toxic dose is 6 times the effective dose. This represents a moderate safety margin. In contrast, digoxin has a TI of approximately 2 — the toxic dose is only twice the effective dose, leaving almost no room for error in dosing or patient variability.

Answer: TI = 6. A higher TI = a safer (more forgiving) drug. Plate 1.2 contrasts a wide versus a narrow therapeutic ratio graphically.

Label Key — Wide vs narrow therapeutic ratio
Wide therapeutic ratio (upper panel)
The desired effect (green) reaches near-100% response well before the adverse effect (blue) curve even begins to rise. There is a large dose range over which the drug is effective but not yet toxic — dosing is forgiving. Examples: most beta-blockers, most macrolide antibiotics.
Narrow therapeutic ratio (lower panel)
The two curves are nearly adjacent — even a small dose increase beyond the effective range produces measurable adverse effects. Drugs like digoxin, lithium, warfarin, theophylline, and aminoglycosides sit in this category. Routine plasma level monitoring is mandatory for these agents.
Desired effect curve (green)
Sigmoidal curve representing the probability of therapeutic benefit at each dose. Its position on the dose axis is determined by ED50.
Adverse effect curve (blue)
Sigmoidal curve for harm. The closer its left foot to the green curve's plateau, the narrower the therapeutic ratio — and the more careful prescribing must be.
Reasoning · Why are dose-response curves sigmoidal?

The S-shape reflects population variability in drug sensitivity. At very low doses, only the most sensitive patients respond; at very high doses, even the least sensitive do. The steep middle section represents the bulk of the normal distribution. This is why TI is defined at the 50% level — it uses the statistical midpoint, avoiding distortion by outliers at either extreme. A steeper sigmoid (more homogeneous population) would give a more reliable TI, but the "real world" curve is always shallower than the textbook version.

Memory hook · Low TI = "DIAL carefully"

Digoxin · Iron · Aminoglycosides · Lithium

All four are classic narrow-TI drugs whose plasma levels must be monitored routinely. Warfarin and phenytoin round out the most-tested list.

§1.2Therapeutic Window

Label Key — Therapeutic window graph
Red curve (Therapeutic response)
Rises steeply then plateaus — the proportion of patients experiencing benefit. Notice it is sigmoidal on a logarithmic concentration axis (as noted in the slide: "the ordinate is linear; the abscissa is logarithmic"). This allows a wide range of concentrations to be displayed.
Black curve (Adverse effects)
A second sigmoid to the right. The leftward shoulder of this curve marks where adverse effects begin to appear — the upper boundary of the therapeutic window.
Therapeutic window (dashed vertical zone)
The shaded region between where the therapeutic response curve achieves meaningful benefit (~1.6 ng/ml in this example) and where adverse effects begin (~3 ng/ml). Keeping plasma concentration in this zone is the goal of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM).
Overlap region (grey shading, ~2.8–3.2 ng/ml)
A small area where adverse effects begin while the therapeutic effect is still rising — the "trading" zone. This is why therapeutic window "does not guarantee safety" — at the upper boundary, a fraction of patients are already experiencing harm.

The therapeutic window differs from the TI: the TI is a population ratio measured in clinical trials, while the therapeutic window is the individual plasma concentration range used to guide dosing in practice. As Plate 1.3 shows, there is always an area of overlap at the upper boundary where therapeutic benefit coexists with emerging toxicity — this is why the therapeutic window "does not guarantee safety and efficacy" but rather indicates where the probability of benefit is maximised and harm minimised.

Clinical context · Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

For narrow-TI drugs, clinicians measure plasma drug levels (TDM) to confirm the patient sits inside the therapeutic window. Key examples: digoxin (target 0.5–2 nmol/L — above this, bradycardia and arrhythmias; below, cardiac failure goes uncontrolled); lithium (0.6–1.0 mmol/L — above 1.5 mmol/L causes coarse tremor, confusion, and renal damage); gentamicin (peak and trough levels to balance bactericidal efficacy against nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity). TDM is not needed for drugs with wide therapeutic ratios (e.g. amoxicillin) where a 10-fold variation in plasma level causes no meaningful change in outcome.

R Recall — §1 Therapeutic Index & Window
  • TI = TD50 / ED50 — higher TI = safer drug; measured at 50% response level
  • Low-TI drugs (DIAL): Digoxin, Iron, Aminoglycosides, Lithium — plus warfarin, phenytoin
  • Therapeutic window = plasma concentration range for benefit with acceptable toxicity (used in TDM)
  • Logarithmic concentration axis is standard for dose-response curves (wide range)
  • A TI of 6 means TD50 = 6 × ED50 (comfortable margin)
§2Adverse Drug Reactions

Adverse Drug Reactions — Classification

Not all drug harms are equal: some are the drug "doing too much", others are the drug doing something entirely unexpected.

An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response to a drug at doses normally used in humans. The most practically useful distinction — and the one tested most often — is between predictable and unpredictable reactions, which correspond to the pharmacological Type A/B framework.

§2.1Type A vs Type B — The Core Distinction

Predictable (Type A) vs Unpredictable (Type B) ADRs
FeatureType A — Predictable (Augmented)Type B — Unpredictable (Bizarre)
MechanismConsequence of the drug's main pharmacological action or known pharmacokineticsUnrelated to the known pharmacological action (off-target, idiosyncratic)
Dose relationshipDose-related — too much drug, or altered PK leading to accumulationNot dose-related — may occur at very low doses
FrequencyCommonLess common, but individually more serious
SeverityOften moderate — manageable by dose reductionOften severe — may require drug withdrawal
PreventabilityMostly preventable and reversibleDifficult to predict; may require prior sensitisation
ExamplesDigoxin toxicity (bradycardia), anticoagulant-induced haemorrhage, hypoglycaemia from insulin overdose, anticholinergic effects of TCAsPenicillin hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis), malignant hyperthermia, idiosyncratic liver failure from halothane
Reasoning · Why are Type A ADRs dose-related?

Type A ADRs are simply the drug "doing too much of what it was designed to do." Warfarin prevents clotting (therapeutic) — at excess levels it prevents all clotting (haemorrhage = Type A). Beta-blockers slow the heart (therapeutic) — excessive blockade causes bradycardia and heart block (Type A). The pharmacological mechanism is the same as the therapeutic effect; only the degree is wrong. This is why Type A ADRs track dose almost perfectly and why reducing the dose usually reverses them. The dose–response curve that produces benefit is the same one that, extended rightward, produces harm.

Reasoning · Why are Type B ADRs unpredictable?

Type B reactions operate via mechanisms that are absent in most people — hence their idiosyncratic nature. Malignant hyperthermia, for example, is caused by a rare mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) that causes uncontrolled calcium release in skeletal muscle when exposed to volatile anaesthetics. Penicillin hypersensitivity occurs when the drug haptenates to plasma proteins, triggering IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation — a process that requires prior sensitisation. No pharmacokinetic calculation can predict either reaction in a naïve patient. Genetic pharmacology (pharmacogenomics) is progressively allowing us to pre-screen for some Type B risk genes.

Clinical example · Low-TI drugs and Type A ADRs

The lecture explicitly notes that "drugs with low therapeutic index are especially likely to be involved in adverse drug reactions." Consider lithium: therapeutic range 0.6–1.0 mmol/L; toxic above 1.5 mmol/L. Because the range is so narrow, any factor that reduces renal clearance — dehydration, NSAIDs (reduce GFR), thiazides (reduce lithium excretion) — can push a stable patient into toxicity without any change in their lithium dose. This is a classic Type A ADR: predictable, dose-related, mechanistically obvious, and (if caught early) reversible by dose reduction and rehydration.

§2.2Full Classification — Rawlins & Thomson

The Rawlins & Thomson framework extends Type A/B to capture a wider range of temporal and mechanistic patterns. Every category has exam-ready examples:

Rawlins & Thomson classification of ADRs
TypeDescriptorMechanism / featureExamples
AAugmented (Dose-related)Consequence of pharmacological action; dose-dependentDigoxin toxicity, SSRI bleeding, TCA anticholinergic effects
BBizarre (Non-dose related)Idiosyncratic or immunological; off-targetPenicillin anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia
CChronic (Dose- & time-related)Requires both cumulative dose and prolonged exposureHypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression by long-term glucocorticoids — endogenous cortisol production fails
DDelayed (Time-related)Appears long after exposure; not dose-related in a simple senseThalidomide-induced phocomelia (teratogenesis), valproate neural tube defects, chemotherapy-related carcinogenesis
EEnd-of-use (Withdrawal)Occurs when a drug is stopped abruptly after physiological dependenceOpiate withdrawal syndrome; beta-blocker withdrawal causing rebound myocardial ischaemia (up-regulation of beta receptors)
FFailure of therapyDrug fails to produce the expected therapeutic effectOral contraceptive failure with enzyme inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort) accelerating hormone metabolism
Clinical importance · HPA axis suppression (Type C)

A patient on long-term prednisolone (glucocorticoids) develops HPA axis suppression: the hypothalamus and pituitary downregulate CRH and ACTH in response to the exogenous steroid signal, so the adrenal glands atrophy. If the steroid is stopped suddenly, there is insufficient endogenous cortisol for physiological stress — producing an Addisonian crisis (hypotension, hypoglycaemia, collapse). This is why glucocorticoids must always be tapered rather than stopped abruptly after prolonged use — the adrenal glands need time to recover. This is a textbook Type C (and arguably Type E) ADR.

R Recall — §2 Adverse Drug Reactions
  • Type A (Predictable/Augmented): dose-related, common, pharmacological mechanism, usually reversible by dose reduction
  • Type B (Unpredictable/Bizarre): not dose-related, idiosyncratic, off-target, often requires drug withdrawal
  • Type C — chronic/cumulative: HPA suppression by glucocorticoids
  • Type D — delayed: thalidomide (teratogenesis), valproate (neural tube defects)
  • Type E — end-of-use withdrawal: opiates, beta-blockers (rebound ischaemia)
  • Type F — failure of therapy: OCP + enzyme inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort)
§3Patient & Drug Factors

Predisposition to ADRs

The same drug, the same dose — but not the same patient. Individual risk factors amplify or dampen ADR probability.

Knowing that a drug has a low TI is necessary but insufficient; you also need to know whether this particular patient handles it differently. The lecture identifies two broad categories of predisposing factors: patient-related and drug-related.

Patient-related risk factors

  • Age extremes — Neonates have immature hepatic CYP450 enzymes and reduced renal GFR; drugs accumulate. Elderly patients have reduced liver mass/blood flow, lower albumin (more free drug), and declining GFR — all of which raise effective plasma drug concentrations.
  • Sex/gender — Women generally have a higher body fat percentage (alters volume of distribution of lipophilic drugs), lower GFR on a weight-adjusted basis, and differences in CYP enzyme activity that affect metabolism of certain drugs.
  • Underlying disease — Hepatic disease reduces first-pass metabolism and drug biotransformation; renal disease reduces drug excretion. Both prolong drug half-lives and raise plasma levels toward toxic territory.
  • Hepatic and renal function — The two primary drug-clearance organs. Impairment of either requires dose adjustment for renally or hepatically cleared drugs.
  • Body weight and fat distribution — Influences volume of distribution (Vd). Lipophilic drugs (e.g. diazepam) accumulate in adipose tissue, prolonging their half-lives in obese patients.
  • Genetic factors — Pharmacogenomic variation in CYP enzymes (e.g. CYP2D6 poor metabolisers accumulate codeine's active metabolite; ultra-metabolisers can achieve opioid toxicity at standard doses), drug transporters, and receptor targets alter individual drug handling profoundly.

Drug-related risk factors

  • Polypharmacy — Multiple drug interactions multiply ADR risk exponentially. The more drugs a patient takes, the greater the chance of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic collisions. This is especially prevalent in the elderly, who often take 5–10+ concurrent medications.
  • Smoking and alcohol — Smoking induces CYP1A2 (lowers theophylline and olanzapine levels). Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 (raises risk of paracetamol hepatotoxicity at even moderate paracetamol doses). Acute alcohol inhibits many CYPs (raises drug levels transiently).
  • Route of administration — IV administration bypasses first-pass metabolism, delivering higher peak plasma levels; increases risk of concentration-related ADRs compared to oral dosing.
  • Dose and frequency — Both influence average steady-state concentration and the risk of exceeding the therapeutic window during peak-dose periods.
Reasoning · Why does polypharmacy amplify ADR risk disproportionately?

With 2 drugs, there is 1 potential interaction pair. With 5 drugs, there are 10 potential pairs. With 10 drugs, there are 45 pairs. This combinatorial explosion means that going from 5 to 10 medications multiplies the number of potential interactions more than fourfold, while each new drug also adds its own direct ADR risk. The elderly — who are the primary polypharmacy population — are simultaneously the most vulnerable to ADRs due to their reduced physiological reserve. Polypharmacy review (medication reconciliation) is one of the highest-yield patient safety interventions.

Clinical example · Renal impairment and digoxin toxicity

Digoxin is renally excreted (approximately 80% unchanged in urine). In a patient with chronic kidney disease whose GFR drops from 90 mL/min to 30 mL/min, digoxin clearance falls by two-thirds. If the dose is not adjusted, plasma digoxin concentration triples — pushing from the therapeutic range (0.5–2 nmol/L) into the toxic range (>2 nmol/L). The patient develops bradycardia, AV block, nausea, and the classic "yellow-green" visual disturbances (xanthopsia). This is a predictable (Type A) ADR in a predisposed patient whose altered renal function was the risk factor.

R Recall — §3 Predisposition to ADRs
  • Patient factors: age extremes, gender, underlying disease, hepatic/renal function, body composition, genetics
  • Drug factors: polypharmacy, smoking/alcohol, route of administration, dose and frequency
  • Polypharmacy — interactions scale combinatorially; especially dangerous in the elderly
  • Renal/hepatic impairment → reduced clearance → drug accumulation → Type A ADR
§4Drug Interactions

Drug–Drug Interactions

Drug-drug interactions account for 10–20% of ADRs — they can cause therapeutic failure, unexpected toxicity, or both.

A drug–drug interaction (DDI) is the modification of the action of one drug by another. As Plates 3.1 and 3.2 show, the four mechanistic categories — behavioural, pharmaceutic, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic — differ fundamentally in where and how the interaction occurs.

Label Key — Drug interaction overview
Drug(s) node (blue-purple box)
Other prescription or OTC drugs — the most clinically common interaction source. Co-administration is the starting point for all DDIs discussed in this lecture.
Food (green box)
Dietary interactions — the most famous being grapefruit juice, which inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, raising plasma levels of numerous drugs (atorvastatin, amlodipine, simvastatin).
Supplement (orange box)
Herbal and nutritional supplements — often overlooked by patients. St John's Wort is a potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inducer; it can cause oral contraceptive failure and reduce antiretroviral levels.
Medical Condition (grey box)
Disease states that alter drug handling — renal/hepatic impairment slowing clearance; cardiac failure reducing hepatic blood flow and first-pass metabolism; hyperthyroidism altering drug metabolism rates.
Decrease action of drug
Leads to therapeutic failure — the drug does not achieve its intended effect because its plasma level is too low or its receptor target is blocked/competed.
Increase action of drug
Leads to toxicity — the drug achieves supraphysiological levels or its effect is amplified beyond the therapeutic window, producing ADRs.
Label Key — Four types of DDI
Behavioural (altered compliance)
Not a pharmacological interaction — one drug affects patient behaviour toward another. Example: sedatives reducing compliance with other medications; alcohol-drug combinations reducing adherence. Less commonly tested but clinically real.
Pharmaceutic (outside the body)
Physical or chemical incompatibility before the drug enters the body: in the IV bag, syringe, or gut lumen. Example: IV precipitate formation if two drugs are mixed. Example: calcium chelating tetracycline in the GI tract (reducing tetracycline absorption).
Pharmacokinetic (altered concentration)
Drug B changes how Drug A is absorbed, distributed, metabolised, or excreted — altering its plasma concentration without directly competing at its target receptor. This is the most clinically important category for narrow-TI drugs.
Pharmacodynamic (altered effect)
Drug B alters the effect of Drug A at the receptor or effector level — even if Drug A's plasma concentration is unchanged. Additive (synergism) or opposing (antagonism) effects at shared or linked pathways.

§4.1Pharmacodynamic Interactions

Pharmacodynamic interactions are the most common type of DDI and usually have a mechanistically simple explanation: two drugs act at the same receptor or on the same effector system, and their effects sum (synergism) or cancel (antagonism).

Label Key — GABA-A receptor binding sites
α subunit (pink, two present)
Contains the benzodiazepine binding site at the α–γ interface. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam) are positive allosteric modulators — they increase the frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening in response to GABA without directly opening the channel themselves. This is why benzodiazepines require GABA to be present to have an effect (and why they are safer than barbiturates in overdose).
β subunit (green, two present)
Contains one of the GABA binding sites at the α–β interface. Also a site of action for neurosteroids (e.g. allopregnanolone) which potentiate GABA-A activity.
γ subunit (white, central)
Required for benzodiazepine sensitivity. Also involved in the ion conduction pore. The γ subunit composition determines which benzodiazepine subtypes are active.
Cl⁻ ion (downward arrow)
The functional output of GABA-A activation: chloride ions flow inward, hyperpolarising the post-synaptic neuron and reducing its probability of firing. More Cl⁻ influx = more CNS depression.
Ethanol
Acts at a hydrophobic site within the channel lumen or at the membrane interface to potentiate GABA-A Cl⁻ influx — the mechanism of alcohol's sedative effects. Combined with benzodiazepines, ethanol produces additive pharmacodynamic CNS depression at the GABA-A receptor.
Barbiturates
Bind to a site on the β subunit; unlike benzodiazepines, they can open the channel directly without GABA, explaining their lower therapeutic index and higher overdose risk.

As Plate 4.1 shows, the GABA-A receptor is the molecular target of multiple CNS depressants that act through distinct binding sites to produce the same net effect — increased Cl⁻ influx and neuronal inhibition. When alcohol and benzodiazepines are taken together, their effects at this receptor are additive: the combined degree of CNS depression can suppress the respiratory drive centre in the brainstem, causing respiratory arrest.

Reasoning · Additive vs synergistic pharmacodynamic interactions

A purely additive interaction is when two drugs each contribute their full effect and the combined outcome equals the sum of the individual effects. A synergistic (supra-additive) interaction occurs when the combined effect exceeds the sum — as can happen when two drugs act at different steps in a shared pathway. In clinical practice, the alcohol-benzodiazepine interaction is treated as additive to synergistic depending on dose and individual variation. Either way, the danger is real. The opposite pattern — two drugs competing for the same receptor — is pharmacodynamic antagonism: beta-blockers competitively block beta-receptors, opposing the bronchodilatory effect of beta-agonists in asthma. Both mechanisms require the same mental model: follow the receptor.

Clinical example · Beta-blockers and beta-agonists in asthma

A patient with both heart failure (on carvedilol, a non-selective beta-blocker) and asthma (on salbutamol, a beta-2 agonist) presents with worsening wheeze. The pharmacodynamic interaction is direct and competitive: carvedilol blocks β2-receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, opposing salbutamol's bronchodilatory action. This interaction can precipitate life-threatening bronchospasm. The preferred approach is to use a cardioselective beta-1 blocker (bisoprolol, metoprolol) which preferentially targets cardiac β1 receptors, leaving β2 receptors relatively free for salbutamol to act. This is a classic pharmacodynamic antagonism interaction with major clinical consequences.

§4.2Pharmacokinetic Interactions

Pharmacokinetic interactions change the amount of drug that reaches its site of action — by altering absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion — without directly touching the receptor.

Absorption interactions

The lecture highlights oral contraceptives and antibiotics as an example of altered bioavailability. The mechanism debated historically is that broad-spectrum antibiotics alter gut flora that recycle oestrogen conjugates via enterohepatic circulation — though this mechanism has been questioned; enzyme induction (rifampicin, below) is a more robust mechanism. Pharmaceutic interactions in the gut (e.g. calcium chelating tetracycline) physically reduce absorption by forming non-absorbable complexes.

Distribution interactions

Displacement of drug from plasma albumin is a classic pharmacokinetic interaction. Highly protein-bound drugs (warfarin is ~99% bound) compete for albumin binding sites. If a second drug displaces even 1% more warfarin from albumin, free warfarin doubles transiently. However, this is usually self-limiting because the increased free drug is also more available for elimination — displacement alone rarely causes sustained toxicity unless clearance is also impaired.

Excretion interactions

Penicillin and probenecid is the landmark example. Probenecid blocks the organic anion transporter (OAT) in the renal proximal tubule that secretes penicillin into the urine. Blocking this transporter reduces renal clearance of penicillin, prolonging its half-life and raising its plasma concentration. This was exploited therapeutically in the 1940s when penicillin was scarce — probenecid was co-administered to maximise the effect of limited penicillin supplies.

§4.3CYP450 — Inducers, Inhibitors & Substrates

Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes in the liver (and gut wall) are responsible for the Phase I metabolism of the majority of drugs in clinical use. Interactions at CYP450 are the most clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction category. The three key roles a drug can play:

Key CYP450 isoforms — Inducers, Inhibitors, and Substrates (from Australian Medicines Handbook)
IsoformInducers (↑ enzyme)Inhibitors (↓ enzyme)Substrates (metabolised by)
CYP1A2 Omeprazole, Tobacco smoking Ciprofloxacin, Fluvoxamine Warfarin, Olanzapine, Bupropion, Codeine, Flecainide
CYP2D6 (few significant inducers) Fluoxetine, Paroxetine, Terbinafine Oxycodone, Amitriptyline, Codeine
CYP3A4/5 Carbamazepine, St John's wort, Rifampicin, Efavirenz Clarithromycin, Fluconazole, Grapefruit juice Warfarin, Atorvastatin, Clopidogrel, Codeine, Diazepam
Reasoning · Why do CYP inducers reduce drug levels, and inhibitors raise them?

CYP enzymes metabolise (break down) drugs — so anything that upregulates these enzymes accelerates drug breakdown, lowering plasma concentration. Inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine) activate the nuclear receptor PXR/CAR, which transcriptionally upregulates CYP450 gene expression over days to weeks — increasing the amount of enzyme available to clear substrates. If warfarin is the substrate, more enzyme = faster warfarin breakdown = lower warfarin levels = loss of anticoagulation (therapeutic failure). Conversely, inhibitors (fluconazole, grapefruit furanocoumarins) block active CYP sites, slowing substrate metabolism. The same warfarin is now degraded more slowly = higher warfarin levels = haemorrhage risk. The key clinical insight: inducers cause underdosing; inhibitors cause overdosing.

Clinical example · Rifampicin + oral contraceptives (OCP) — Type F ADR

Rifampicin is one of the most potent known CYP3A4 inducers (and also induces P-glycoprotein). A woman stable on the combined OCP who starts rifampicin for tuberculosis will experience dramatically accelerated metabolism of oestrogen and progesterone. Plasma hormone levels fall below the contraceptive threshold, and unintended pregnancy can occur despite "correct" pill use. This is classified as a Type F ADR — unexpected failure of therapy due to a drug interaction. The solution is to use a non-hormonal contraception method (barrier, IUD) during rifampicin therapy and for 4–8 weeks after it is stopped (until CYP induction reverses).

Memory hook · CYP3A4 inducers — "PC BRES"

Phenytoin · Carbamazepine · Barbiturates · Rifampicin · Efavirenz · St John's wort

All are potent CYP3A4 inducers that reduce levels of their substrates (warfarin, statins, OCP, antiretrovirals, tacrolimus). Grapefruit is the famous CYP3A4 inhibitor — it does the opposite.

R Recall — §4 Drug–Drug Interactions
  • DDIs in 10–20% of ADRs — especially common in elderly polypharmacy patients
  • Four DDI mechanisms: Behavioural · Pharmaceutic · Pharmacokinetic · Pharmacodynamic
  • Pharmacodynamic: synergism (alcohol + benzodiazepines → GABA-A additive CNS depression) or antagonism (beta-blockers vs beta-agonists)
  • CYP inducers → reduce substrate levels → therapeutic failure (Rifampicin + warfarin/OCP)
  • CYP inhibitors → raise substrate levels → toxicity (Fluconazole + warfarin → haemorrhage)
  • Grapefruit juice → irreversibly inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → raises atorvastatin, amlodipine etc.
  • Penicillin + probenecid: probenecid blocks renal OAT → reduces penicillin excretion → prolongs penicillin action
  • Codeine: prodrug activated by CYP2D6; CYP2D6 poor metabolisers get no analgesia; ultra-rapid metabolisers get toxicity
§5Toxicology

Poisoning & Toxicology Management

"All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison." — Paracelsus, 16th century.

A poison is any substance — including any drug — that has the capacity to harm a living organism. Poisoning is exposure to pharmaceuticals, illicit drugs, or chemicals leading to damaging physiological effects. Management follows a structured four-stage framework: Assess, Prevent further absorption, Increase elimination, and Deploy specific antidotes.

§5.1Assessment of the Poisoned Patient

The first question is not "what is the antidote?" but "what is happening right now?" The initial assessment of a poisoned patient is clinical and systematic:

  • What drug(s)? — Identify the agent(s) from the history, pill bottles, witnesses, or clinical syndrome (toxidrome).
  • How much? — Estimate dose ingested; correlate with known toxic thresholds.
  • How long since ingestion? — Determines whether gut decontamination (activated charcoal) is still effective (most effective within 1 hour), and informs the expected time course of toxicity and its peak.
  • Clinical parameters: Level of consciousness (GCS), respiratory rate and depth, blood pressure, and body temperature are the four vital parameters that determine immediate threat to life and guide resuscitation.
Reasoning · Why does time since ingestion matter so much?

Gut decontamination methods (activated charcoal, gastric lavage) are only effective while the drug is still in the gastrointestinal tract and has not been absorbed into the bloodstream. Most drugs are absorbed within 1–4 hours of ingestion; modified-release formulations may delay this. After absorption is complete, the focus shifts entirely to supporting physiology, increasing elimination, and giving antidotes. Activated charcoal given after 4 hours is largely futile for most immediate-release formulations. Time is therefore not merely a clinical variable — it directly determines the treatment options available.

§5.2Management Principles & Specific Antidotes

Label Key — Poisoning management flowchart (Plate 5.1)
Assessment & examination (central teal box, top)
The starting point: gather information (what drug, how much, how long ago) and assess the patient's current physiological status (consciousness, respiration, BP, temperature). These inputs determine the urgency and direct the subsequent management steps.
Prevent further absorption (central teal box, middle)
Two methods: Activated charcoal — a highly porous carbon preparation that adsorbs drugs in the gut lumen, preventing their absorption into the bloodstream. Must be given early (within 1 hour for most drugs). Gastric lavage — physical washout of stomach contents via a nasogastric tube; now rarely used and considered controversial because aspiration risk may outweigh benefit.
Specific antidotes (central teal box, third)
Targeted pharmacological reversal of the toxin's mechanism. Dashed arrow to left panel indicates the antidotes listed are each specific to their named toxin. Only used when an effective antidote exists and the clinical picture warrants it.
Increase elimination (central teal box, bottom)
Three strategies: Repeated-dose activated charcoal — given every 4 hours, acts as "gastrointestinal dialysis" by adsorbing drug secreted back into the gut lumen (enterohepatic recirculation). Alkaline diuresis — IV sodium bicarbonate alkalinises urine, ionising weak-acid drugs (salicylates, phenobarbital) and trapping them in tubular fluid, preventing reabsorption. Haemodialysis — mechanically filters the bloodstream; effective for small, water-soluble, low-protein-bound drugs (salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol). Charcoal haemoperfusion — blood is passed through an activated charcoal column; removes protein-bound drugs not well cleared by haemodialysis (theophylline, barbiturates).
Antidotes panel (left, blue border)
Lists the specific antidote for each major toxin class — these must be memorised as fact-pairs (see table below).
Toxin analysis panels (right)
Purple box: drugs measurable by toxicology screen on admission (paracetamol, iron, lithium, salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol). Orange box: drugs for which repeated-dose charcoal is used (carbamazepine, theophylline, digoxin, salicylates). Green box: drugs treated by haemodialysis (salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol). Red box: drugs treated by charcoal haemoperfusion (theophylline, barbiturates).

Specific antidotes — must-know pairs

Specific antidotes and their mechanisms
ToxinAntidoteMechanism of antidote action
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) N-Acetylcysteine (acetylcysteine) IV; Methionine p.o. Replenishes glutathione stores → prevents accumulation of NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine), the reactive metabolite that covalently binds hepatocyte proteins → prevents hepatic necrosis. Must be given within 8–10 hours for maximal effect.
Opioids Naloxone IV/IM/IN Competitive antagonist at μ, κ, and δ opioid receptors — displaces the opioid from receptors, rapidly reversing respiratory depression, sedation, and miosis. Half-life ~60–90 minutes (shorter than most opioids — re-dosing or infusion often needed).
Iron Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine) IV Chelating agent — binds free ferric iron (Fe³⁺) in the bloodstream, forming ferrioxamine complex that is renally excreted. Prevents iron from generating reactive oxygen species (Fenton reaction → OH• → cellular damage).
Methanol & Ethylene glycol Ethanol IV (historically) or Fomepizole IV (preferred) Both inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing conversion of methanol to formic acid (causes optic nerve damage) and ethylene glycol to oxalate (causes renal failure). Fomepizole is a direct ADH inhibitor; ethanol competes as an alternative substrate.
Organophosphorus insecticides Atropine + Pralidoxime Atropine: muscarinic antagonist — blocks excessive ACh stimulation at muscarinic receptors (DUMBELS syndrome: Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation). Pralidoxime: reactivates acetylcholinesterase by displacing the organophosphate before it "ages" (irreversibly binds) — must be given early.
Carbon monoxide 100% O₂; Hyperbaric O₂ in severe cases CO binds haemoglobin with ~240× greater affinity than O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb). High-flow O₂ dramatically shortens the half-life of COHb (from ~5 hours in air to ~60 min on 100% O₂; ~20 min hyperbaric).
Lead / Mercury Chelating agents (DMSA, D-penicillamine, EDTA) Chelators bind heavy metal ions, forming water-soluble complexes excreted renally. Different chelators are preferred for different metals — choice depends on metal and severity.
Reasoning · Why does paracetamol overdose cause liver failure (and why does N-acetylcysteine work)?

At therapeutic doses, paracetamol is ~95% conjugated (glucuronidation and sulphation) and ~5% converted by CYP2E1/CYP3A4 to NAPQI — a highly reactive electrophile. At therapeutic doses, NAPQI is rapidly detoxified by conjugation with hepatic glutathione. In overdose, the conjugation pathways are saturated and NAPQI production overwhelms glutathione stores; free NAPQI then covalently modifies cysteine residues of hepatic proteins and mitochondrial components, causing hepatocyte necrosis. Importantly, chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1, increasing NAPQI production — explaining why alcoholics are at risk of liver failure even at "moderate" paracetamol doses. N-acetylcysteine works because it is a glutathione precursor: it replenishes the store that detoxifies NAPQI. Time is critical because once hepatocyte damage is established, even more NAC cannot reverse it.

Clinical example · Alkaline diuresis for salicylate poisoning

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) overdose causes a mixed acid-base picture: an early respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory centre) and a later metabolic acidosis (accumulation of salicylate and its metabolites). The management principle for moderate salicylate toxicity is alkaline diuresis: IV sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) is infused to raise urine pH above 7.5. Salicylate is a weak acid (pKa ~3). In alkaline urine, it is almost entirely ionised (salicylate⁻) — the ionised form cannot cross the lipid bilayer of tubular epithelial cells back into the bloodstream. It is trapped in the tubular lumen and excreted in the urine, dramatically increasing clearance. This is the ion-trapping principle: alkaline urine accelerates elimination of weak acids; acidic urine would be used (theoretically) for weak bases.

Clinical example · Opioid overdose — the naloxone time-trap

A 35-year-old is brought in unconscious after suspected heroin overdose. Naloxone 0.4 mg IV is given — within 2 minutes the patient is awake, breathing normally, and attempting to leave. Thirty minutes later, they are found unconscious again. Why? Heroin is rapidly converted in vivo to morphine, which has a longer duration of action than naloxone. Naloxone's half-life is only 60–90 minutes; as it wears off, opioid receptor activity returns and respiratory depression recurs. The clinical rule: naloxone duration is often shorter than the opioid's action — patients must be monitored, and repeat doses or a naloxone infusion may be required.

R Recall — §5 Poisoning & Toxicology
  • Assessment: What drug? How much? How long ago? LOC, respiration, BP, temperature
  • Prevent absorption: Activated charcoal (within 1 hour); gastric lavage (rarely used, controversial)
  • Increase elimination: Repeated-dose charcoal (GI dialysis — theophylline, digoxin, carbamazepine); Alkaline diuresis NaHCO₃ (salicylates, phenobarbital); Haemodialysis (salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol); Charcoal haemoperfusion (theophylline, barbiturates)
  • Antidotes: Naloxone (opioids) · Acetylcysteine (paracetamol/NAPQI) · Desferrioxamine (iron) · Atropine + Pralidoxime (organophosphates) · Fomepizole/ethanol (methanol/ethylene glycol — inhibit ADH) · O₂/hyperbaric O₂ (CO) · Chelators (lead/mercury)
  • Paracetamol mechanism: CYP → NAPQI → glutathione depletion → hepatocyte necrosis; NAC replenishes glutathione
  • Ion-trapping: Alkaline urine ionises weak acids (salicylate) → prevents tubular reabsorption → ↑ excretion
  • Naloxone caveat: shorter half-life than most opioids — repeat doses or infusion may be needed
